lessons.title: Engineering Processes — Marking, Cutting, Shaping & Drilling

before.content_html:
From Raw Material to Finished Part

Engineering is the process of turning raw material into a finished product. Almost every product requires a sequence of operations: first the material is prepared, then marked out, then cut and shaped, then drilled or turned, and finally finished. Each stage removes material or changes its form. Choosing the correct process for each stage — and the correct tool for each process — is a core engineering skill.

The specification groups processes into categories: material removal (cutting, filing, drilling), shaping and manipulation (turning, milling, forming), and preparation and finishing. This lesson covers the first two categories and the key tools associated with them. Joining and finishing are covered in the next lesson.

Marking Out

Marking out is the first operation on a new piece of material. Before any cutting takes place, the engineer transfers the dimensions from the drawing onto the material surface. This ensures that cuts are made in the right place and that the finished part will be within the required tolerance.

The key marking-out tools are:

  • A scriber — a hardened steel pointed tool used to scratch fine lines onto metal. It works like a pencil on metal, leaving a thin precise line that can be seen when cutting.
  • A centre punch — used to make a small indentation exactly where a hole is to be drilled. The indent stops the drill bit from wandering off the marked position when it first contacts the material.
  • A try-square (engineers’ square) — used to check that lines are at right angles to a reference edge. Accurate right angles are essential for most engineering components.
  • Vernier calipers and a steel rule — used to measure and transfer dimensions. A vernier caliper can measure internal and external dimensions to a high degree of precision.
Key Fact

The purpose of the centre punch is often misunderstood in exams. It does not mark a line — it creates a small indent that acts as a starting point for the drill bit. Without it, the drill bit will skate across the surface instead of cutting in the intended location.

Cutting

Cutting removes material by shearing it with a blade. The choice of cutting tool depends on the material type, the thickness of the material, and the complexity of the cut required.

A hacksaw is the standard hand tool for cutting metal, plastic and other hard materials. The blade is held in tension in a frame, which keeps it straight during the cut. Fine-tooth blades are used for thin sections and hard materials; coarser blades for thicker, softer stock. A hacksaw is slow but precise and requires no power supply.

A bandsaw is a power tool that uses a continuous loop of toothed blade running between two wheels. It can cut through thicker material much faster than a hacksaw and is especially useful for curved cuts. Bandsaws must be guarded correctly and the operator’s hands must never be in line with the blade.

Filing

Filing removes small amounts of material using a hardened steel file. It is used to smooth rough cut edges, bring a part to its final dimension, and remove burrs left by cutting. Files are classified by their cut (the pattern and spacing of the teeth) — a flat smooth file produces a finer surface finish than a flat bastard file, which removes material more quickly. Filing also removes the sharp burrs left on cut edges, which are a safety hazard and would cause injury if left on a finished product.

Drilling

Drilling creates circular holes in material using a rotating drill bit. In a school or college workshop, the most common machine used is the pillar drill (also called a bench drill or pedestal drill). The workpiece is clamped to the table and the drill bit is lowered into the material by a lever or quill feed. The pillar drill is safer than a hand drill for engineering work because the workpiece is clamped and the drill bit moves vertically in a controlled path — the operator’s hands are not near the rotating bit.

The drill speed must be set appropriately for the material being drilled. Softer materials generally require faster speeds; harder materials and larger drill bits require slower speeds to avoid overheating and breaking the drill bit. Engineers consult speed tables (often provided on data sheets) to select the correct speed.

Task: Drill a 6 mm hole in a piece of mild steel plate at a marked position.

Step 1 — Mark and punch: Use a scriber to mark the hole position from the engineering drawing. Use a centre punch and hammer to create a small indent at the marked point. This gives the drill bit a starting location and prevents it wandering.

Step 2 — Set up the machine: Select the correct drill speed for a 6 mm bit in mild steel (consult the speed table). Fit the 6 mm twist drill bit in the chuck and tighten the chuck key. Remove the chuck key before switching the machine on.

Step 3 — Clamp the workpiece: Clamp the steel plate firmly to the pillar drill table using a machine vice or clamps. Never hold the workpiece by hand — if the drill bit snags, the workpiece will spin and cause injury.

Step 4 — Drill the hole: Switch on the machine. Lower the drill bit slowly into the punched indent using the quill feed lever. Apply steady downward pressure. Use a cutting fluid or lubricant to reduce heat and prolong drill bit life when drilling metal. Do not force the drill bit.

Step 5 — De-burr: Switch off and wait for the spindle to stop fully before removing the workpiece. Use a de-burring tool or file to remove the sharp burr around the edge of the hole.

Turning on a Lathe

A centre lathe is used for turning — producing cylindrical, conical and threaded shapes from round bar stock. The workpiece is held in a rotating chuck; the cutting tool is mounted in a tool post and fed into the workpiece. A lathe can face off (produce a flat end), turn down a diameter, drill along the axis, cut threads, and produce tapers. The cutting tool must be set at the correct height and feed rate, and the lathe must not be operated without the appropriate guards in place.

A milling machine uses a rotating multi-tooth cutter to remove material from the top or sides of a workpiece. The workpiece is clamped to a table that moves in the X, Y and Z directions, allowing flat surfaces, slots and complex profiles to be produced. Slot milling cuts a channel into a surface; end milling removes material from the side of the workpiece. Unlike a lathe, where the workpiece rotates, on a milling machine the cutter rotates and the workpiece moves.

Shaping in its broadest engineering sense also includes forming processes such as bending sheet metal around a former or in a sheet metal bender. These processes do not remove material — they change the shape by plastic deformation. They are classified under shaping and manipulation rather than material removal.

Key Fact

On a lathe, the workpiece rotates and the cutting tool is fixed — used for cylindrical shapes. On a milling machine, the cutter rotates and the workpiece moves — used for flat surfaces, slots and profiles. Mixing these up is a common exam error.

lessons.title: Joining & Finishing — Permanent and Temporary Fixings

before.content_html:
Why Joining Matters

Very few engineering products are made from a single piece of material. Almost every product — from a bicycle frame to a circuit board — is an assembly of parts that must be joined together. The method of joining has a direct effect on the strength of the assembly, how easy it is to take apart for maintenance, and what materials can be joined. Choosing the wrong joining method can result in a product that fails in service or cannot be repaired.

Permanent and Temporary Fixings

Permanent fixings are used when the joint will not need to be dismantled. Welding, brazing and riveting all produce permanent joints. A riveted aircraft fuselage panel is not intended to be removed — the rivet must be drilled out if the panel needs replacing, which damages the rivet and sometimes the surrounding material.

Temporary fixings allow parts to be dismantled and reassembled. Nuts and bolts are the most common example: tightening the nut clamps the parts together; loosening it allows disassembly. Screws, machine screws and set screws also provide temporary fixings. These are essential in products that need regular maintenance — a car engine must be taken apart for servicing, so its major components are bolted together, not welded.

Key Fact

The key question when choosing between permanent and temporary fixings is: “Will this joint ever need to be taken apart?” If the answer is no, a permanent method may be stronger and more reliable. If maintenance or replacement is expected, a temporary fixing preserves the ability to disassemble without damage.

Soldering

Soldering uses a low-melting-point filler alloy to join metal parts. The key characteristic of soldering is that the filler melts below 450°C and the parent metals do not melt at all — they remain solid throughout. A soldering iron heats the joint and melts the solder, which flows into the gap by capillary action and solidifies as a permanent joint on cooling. Soldering is used widely in electronics to join components to printed circuit boards, and in plumbing for copper pipe joints.

A flux is applied to the joint area before soldering. Flux prevents oxidation of the metal surfaces during heating, which would prevent the solder from bonding. Without flux, the solder will bead up on an oxidised surface rather than flowing into the joint.

Brazing

Brazing is similar in principle to soldering, but the filler alloy has a melting point above 450°C. This higher temperature produces a stronger joint than soldering. In a school workshop, brazing is carried out on a brazing hearth. The parts are heated by a gas torch until the parent metal is hot enough to melt the brazing rod when it is touched to the joint. The filler flows by capillary action into the gap. Flux is also required in brazing to prevent oxidation.

Because brazing temperatures are higher than soldering temperatures, it is important that the parent metals have melting points well above the brazing filler — otherwise the parent metal itself would melt. For this reason, brazing is more suitable for steel and copper components than for aluminium, which has a lower melting point.

Soldering: Filler melts below 450°C. Parent metals stay solid. Used for electronics and light copper plumbing. Produces the weakest joint of the three.

Brazing: Filler melts above 450°C. Parent metals stay solid. Produces a stronger joint than soldering. Used for steel and copper fabrication in a workshop setting. Requires a gas torch and brazing hearth.

Welding: The parent metals themselves are melted together (with or without a filler rod). Produces the strongest joint because the parent metals fuse. MIG welding (Metal Inert Gas) uses a continuously fed wire electrode and a shielding gas to protect the weld pool. Welding requires more specialist equipment and produces more intense heat, UV radiation and fumes than brazing or soldering.

Exam trap: students often state that brazing “melts the metals together” like welding. This is wrong — in brazing the parent metals do not melt. The filler melts and bonds to the solid parent metal surfaces.

Heat Treatment

Heat treatment changes the properties of a metal by carefully controlling heating and cooling. Three processes are named in the specification:

  • Annealing — the metal is heated to a high temperature and then allowed to cool very slowly (often left inside the furnace or buried in sand). This softens the metal and removes internal stresses, making it more ductile and easier to work. Copper work-hardens as it is hammered; annealing restores its softness.
  • Hardening — steel is heated until it reaches the correct temperature range (the metal glows a specific colour) and then quenched (plunged rapidly into water or oil). This rapid cooling ‘traps’ the structure of the steel in a hard but brittle state. Hardening is used for cutting tools that need to resist wear.
  • Tempering — hardened steel is often too brittle for practical use. Tempering reheats the hardened steel to a lower temperature and then allows it to cool in air. This reduces brittleness while keeping much of the hardness gained during hardening. Tool steel is hardened and then tempered to give the correct balance of hardness and toughness.

Finishing processes protect the surface of a material or improve its appearance. The specification lists painting, plating and polishing as key examples.

Painting: A coating of paint applied to protect against corrosion and to provide colour. Steel must be painted or coated to prevent rusting in damp conditions. The surface must be clean and free from oil before painting, otherwise the paint will not adhere properly.

Plating: A thin layer of one metal is deposited onto the surface of another. Electroplating uses an electric current to deposit the plating metal; hot-dip galvanising coats steel with zinc by dipping it in molten zinc. Zinc plating (galvanising) is widely used on steel components that will be used outdoors because zinc corrodes preferentially to steel, protecting the steel underneath.

Polishing: Abrasive polishing smooths and brightens a metal surface. It may be functional (removing surface roughness to reduce friction) or cosmetic (improving appearance). A buffer or polisher machine uses a rotating abrasive pad or cloth wheel to achieve a high-gloss finish.

Chemical treatment (etching): Chemical etching is used in electronics manufacturing to remove unwanted copper from a PCB (printed circuit board), leaving only the required circuit tracks. It is also used to create a key (rough surface) on metals before painting.

Key Fact

Hardening and tempering are always done in sequence: harden first (heat and quench), then temper (reheat to a lower temperature and air-cool). Tempering without prior hardening does not give the desired result. The purpose of tempering is to reduce the brittleness introduced by rapid quenching.

glossary_terms.definition: A joining method that cannot be reversed without damaging one or both of the parts being joined.
A joining method that allows the parts to be separated and reassembled without damage.
A joining process that uses a filler alloy with a melting point below 450°C to bond materials; the parent metals do not melt.
A joining process that uses a brass or copper-based filler alloy with a melting point above 450°C; the parent metals do not melt.
A refractory-lined work surface used in a workshop for brazing, with fire bricks to reflect heat onto the joint.
A heat treatment process in which a metal is heated and then allowed to cool slowly, reducing hardness and increasing ductility.
A handheld heated tool used to melt solder and transfer it to a joint between electronic components.

before.content_html:
Why Safe Working Matters

Engineering workshops contain real risks: rotating machinery, sharp tools, hot flames, electrical equipment and heavy materials. Every year people are seriously injured in workshops through unsafe practice. Safe working is not an add-on to engineering — it is a fundamental part of the engineer’s job. In a professional engineering company, failure to follow safe working procedures can result in criminal prosecution under health and safety law. In a school or college workshop, the same principles apply.

The legal framework for workplace health and safety in the UK begins with the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974. This Act places a duty on employers to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health, safety and welfare of their employees. It also places duties on employees to take reasonable care of themselves and others, and to cooperate with their employer’s safety arrangements. Two important sets of regulations made under this Act are the Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998 (PUWER) and the Personal Protective Equipment at Work Regulations 1992.

Key Fact

A risk assessment is a systematic process with three stages: (1) identify the hazards; (2) assess the risk (likelihood and severity of harm); (3) decide and implement control measures. You must be able to distinguish between a hazard and a risk — they are not the same thing.

Hazard and Risk: The Critical Distinction

A hazard is anything with the potential to cause harm. A spinning lathe chuck is a hazard. A bottle of solvent is a hazard. A trailing power cable on the workshop floor is a hazard. The hazard exists regardless of whether anyone is actually harmed.

Risk is the combination of two factors: how likely is it that the hazard will actually cause harm, and how severe would that harm be? A spinning lathe chuck has a high severity (the injury would be serious) but a lower likelihood if the operator is trained and the guard is in place. A risk assessment evaluates both factors together. A risk that is highly likely and would cause severe injury requires urgent control measures; a risk that is unlikely and would cause only minor harm may be managed with a simple safety rule.

Task: Drill a 10 mm hole in a piece of mild steel using a pillar drill.

Step 1 — Identify hazards:
• Rotating drill bit (contact causes lacerations or amputation).
• Workpiece snagging and spinning (impact injury to hands and body).
• Metal swarf/cuttings ejected from the hole (eye injury).
• Loose clothing or hair drawn into the spindle (entanglement, severe injury).
• Noise from machine operation (hearing damage with prolonged exposure).

Step 2 — Assess risk (likelihood × severity for each):
Workpiece spinning: HIGH severity (broken bones, lacerations), HIGH likelihood if not clamped → HIGH risk. Must be controlled before work begins.
Eye injury from swarf: MEDIUM severity (could cause permanent eye damage), MEDIUM likelihood without eye protection → MEDIUM-HIGH risk.

Step 3 — Control measures:
• Clamp the workpiece in a machine vice secured to the drill table — eliminates the snagging/spinning hazard.
• Wear safety goggles — reduces the risk of eye injury from swarf.
• Tie back long hair; tuck in loose clothing and remove jewellery — eliminates entanglement risk.
• Ensure the drill guard is in position before switching on — reduces contact risk with the rotating bit.
• Remove the chuck key before switching the machine on — eliminates chuck-key ejection hazard.

The Hierarchy of Control Measures

Control measures are ranked in a hierarchy of control from most effective to least effective. The hierarchy must be applied in order: always seek the highest-level control measure possible before resorting to a lower one.

  • Elimination — remove the hazard entirely. If a task can be redesigned so that the hazard does not exist, this is always the best option. For example, if a chemical solvent is not needed for a task, not using it eliminates the hazard.
  • Substitution — replace the hazard with something less dangerous. Replace a highly toxic solvent with a less hazardous cleaning agent. Replace a sharp metal burr with a plastic edge protector.
  • Engineering controls — use physical barriers or design changes to separate people from the hazard. Machine guards, interlocks (the machine cannot start with the guard open), extraction systems for fumes and dust, and Local Exhaust Ventilation (LEV) are all engineering controls. They are built into the machine or the workplace — they do not depend on the operator remembering to do something.
  • Administrative controls — use rules, training, signage and working procedures to reduce the likelihood of harm. Safe operating procedures, induction training, warning signs and permit-to-work systems are administrative controls. They rely on people following rules, which makes them less reliable than engineering controls.
  • Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) — provide protective equipment such as safety goggles, gloves, ear defenders, safety footwear and overalls. PPE is the last line of defence — it protects only the individual wearing it and does nothing to reduce the hazard itself. It should be used in conjunction with higher-level controls, not as a substitute for them.
Key Fact

Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) is always the last resort in the control hierarchy, not the first. Examiners expect you to recognise that putting on goggles is less effective than fitting a machine guard. A top-band answer will state the hierarchy principle, not just list PPE items.

Common PPE in a Workshop

Different tasks require different PPE. Choosing the correct PPE for the task is a skill in itself. Safety goggles protect eyes from swarf, chips and chemical splashes; face shields provide greater coverage for grinding operations. Ear defenders reduce the risk of hearing damage in noisy workshops. Gloves protect hands from cuts and chemical exposure, but must not be worn when using a lathe or drill — they can snag on the rotating parts and pull the hand in. Heat-resistant gloves are needed when brazing or welding. Safety footwear (steel toe-capped boots) protects against dropped materials. Overalls or workshop coats keep loose clothing away from machinery.

Lathe: Never use a file on a rotating lathe workpiece by holding the file in both hands across the rotating part — this risks the file snagging and pulling your arm into the lathe. Remove all swarf with a brush, not by hand. Ensure the chuck guard is in place. Never wear gloves when operating a lathe.

Pillar drill: Always clamp the workpiece — never hold it by hand. Remove the chuck key before switching on. Lower the guard before starting. Wear goggles. Keep hands clear of the spindle during operation.

Brazing hearth: Work in a well-ventilated area or use LEV (extraction) to remove brazing fumes, which can be harmful if inhaled. Wear appropriate eye protection (tinted goggles or a face shield). Use heat-resistant gloves when handling hot workpieces. Allow workpieces to cool fully before handling with bare hands — hot metal looks the same as cold metal.

Bandsaw: Keep fingers well clear of the blade. Use a push stick for narrow pieces. Do not attempt to back out of a cut while the blade is running. Ensure the blade guard is set as close to the workpiece as practicable to minimise the exposed blade length.

glossary_terms.term: Health and Safety at Work Act 1974
glossary_terms.definition: The primary UK legislation governing health and safety at work, placing duties on employers, employees and others.
A systematic process of identifying hazards in a workplace, assessing the risk they pose, and deciding what control measures are needed to reduce that risk.
Anything with the potential to cause harm to a person.
The likelihood and severity of harm actually occurring as a result of a hazard.
Equipment worn by a person to protect against risks to health and safety, such as safety goggles, gloves or ear defenders.
A ranked order of control measures from most to least effective: elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls, then PPE.
